name: OMK 2A Psych Exam 2 — Batch 3: Anxiety, OCD & Trauma-Related Disorders + Psychotherapy & Theory

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 4-month history of episodes of pounding heartbeat, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, and a sense that she is about to die. Each episode begins abruptly, peaks within about 3 minutes, and resolves within 15 minutes. She has had roughly two episodes weekly; three have awakened her from sleep and others have occurred while she was watching television at home. For the past 6 weeks she has stopped driving on the highway and has declined a promotion that would require travel, because she is preoccupied with when the next episode will strike. She denies fear of being watched or judged, and she reports no worry about her finances, her family, or her health between episodes. Temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 76/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration, electrocardiogram, and urine toxicology screening are normal. On mental status examination, affect is anxious but full-range and thought process is linear. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A panic attack is a discrete surge of intense fear with abrupt onset that peaks within 30 seconds to 5 minutes and includes ≥4 of 13 symptoms — but an attack alone is not panic disorder, because attacks also occur in GAD, OCD, social phobia, and PTSD. Panic disorder requires recurrent attacks that are at least partly unexpected, PLUS ≥1 month of persistent worry about further attacks or a maladaptive behavior change. Her attacks are uncued (nocturnal, and while watching television at home), and the 6 weeks of avoidance and preoccupation satisfy the behavioral criterion. Board pearl — nocturnal attacks are nearly diagnostic of the uncued pattern, since there is no external situation present to cue them.  [Learning objectives: LO 036]

wrongExplanations.0: Agoraphobia requires fear across multiple situations united by the theme that escape or help might be unavailable. Her avoidance of highway driving is a downstream consequence of the attacks rather than a primary fear of being trapped, and no other agoraphobic situations are described. DSM-5 unlinked agoraphobia from panic disorder, so it must stand on its own criteria.
wrongExplanations.1: Generalized anxiety disorder requires excessive, difficult-to-control worry about multiple everyday domains for more than 6 months. She explicitly reports no worry about finances, family, or health between episodes — that stated negative is what closes this option.
wrongExplanations.2: Illness anxiety disorder centers on persistent preoccupation with having a serious illness despite reassurance and minimal somatic symptoms. Her fear is of the attacks themselves recurring, not of an undiagnosed disease, and her somatic symptoms are prominent rather than minimal.
wrongExplanations.4: Social anxiety disorder requires the fear to be of scrutiny and negative evaluation by others. She specifically denies fear of being watched or judged, and several attacks occurred alone at home or during sleep.
wrongExplanations.5: A specific phobia is cued reliably by one discrete object or situation. Attacks that awaken her from sleep cannot be cued by any external stimulus, which rules out a phobic pattern.

questions.eli5: Her panic episodes come out of nowhere — some even wake her up at night — and now she spends her time dreading the next one and avoiding the highway. Attacks that arrive with no trigger, plus a month of worrying about them, is what makes it panic disorder rather than just panic attacks.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of chest tightness, palpitations, shortness of breath, and lightheadedness. He states this is his third such episode in 2 months, that each begins abruptly, and that a physician at an urgent care center told him after the first one that he was 'just having panic attacks.' Tonight's episode began 50 minutes ago and has not let up. He has no history of cardiac or pulmonary disease, takes no medications, and does not use tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drugs. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 194/min and regular, respirations are 22/min, blood pressure is 104/68 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. Lungs are clear and there is no calf tenderness or asymmetric swelling. Urine toxicology screening is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
choices: E. Screening with the GAD-7 questionnaire
questions.explanation: The prior label of 'panic attacks' is the dramatic decoy; two buried clues override it. A true panic attack peaks within 30 seconds to 5 minutes and resolves in minutes — this episode has run 50 minutes without letting up — and a regular rate of 194/min is far outside what anxiety produces. MI, angina, pulmonary embolism, and arrhythmia must be excluded before anything is called 'just panic,' and a sustained regular narrow-complex tachycardia at this rate points to supraventricular tachycardia. A 12-lead ECG is immediate, noninvasive, and the only listed test that captures the rhythm while it is still present. Board pearl — patients routinely misremember attacks as far longer than they were, so a genuinely documented long episode with an extreme heart rate should move you off the psychiatric label.  [Learning objectives: LO 050, 099]

wrongExplanations.0: A Holter monitor records over the following 24 hours and would miss the arrhythmia occurring in front of you right now. Ambulatory monitoring is for capturing intermittent events between episodes, not for a patient who is symptomatic at a rate of 194/min.
wrongExplanations.1: Pulmonary embolism belongs on the differential, but his lungs are clear, oxygen saturation is 99% on room air, and there is no calf tenderness or asymmetric swelling — and CT angiography is a contrast study that should not precede a 30-second bedside test that will likely give the diagnosis.
wrongExplanations.3: Thyrotoxicosis can mimic panic and is worth checking, but a send-out laboratory test does not address a patient in a sustained tachycardia at 194/min during this visit.
wrongExplanations.4: The GAD-7 is a screening instrument for generalized anxiety disorder, not a diagnostic step, and administering a questionnaire to a patient in an active tachyarrhythmia accepts the psychiatric label that the vital signs are arguing against.

questions.eli5: Someone already told him these were panic attacks, but a real panic attack peaks in a few minutes and this one has lasted almost an hour with his heart at 194. Before calling it anxiety, you get a heart tracing while it is still happening.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old high school teacher comes to the office because of a 4-year history of intense fear of being scrutinized and judged. He teaches five class periods daily and reports sweating, trembling, and a racing heart in every one of them; he has twice left mid-lesson. The same fear occurs at weekly faculty meetings, at parent conferences, at restaurants where he might be seen eating, and at family gatherings, and he has declined all social invitations for the past 2 years. He states that he wishes he could take part in these things. He denies obsessions, compulsions, and unexpected attacks occurring outside social situations. He has no cardiac or pulmonary disease, does not use alcohol or illicit drugs, and takes no medications. Pulse is 72/min and blood pressure is 120/78 mm Hg; physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term pharmacotherapy?
choices: A. Alprazolam as needed before each class
B. Atenolol as needed before each class
C. Hydroxyzine as needed for anxiety
D. Propranolol as needed before each class
questions.explanation: The decisive variable is exposure frequency, not the diagnosis. This is generalized social anxiety disorder — the fear spans teaching, meetings, conferences, eating in public, and family gatherings — and he faces it five times every school day. For chronic, daily exposure, serotonergic therapy is the core treatment: an SSRI, or buspirone, paired with CBT and assertiveness training. Board pearl — the exam reading rule is daily fear gets an SSRI, date-night fear gets a beta-blocker. Questions of this type deliberately list both a serotonergic and an as-needed option and test whether you noticed how often the patient is actually exposed.  [Learning objectives: LO 036, 081]

wrongExplanations.0: Alprazolam has the shortest half-life and the highest abuse potential of the benzodiazepines, and dependence can develop in as little as 2 weeks. Dosing it before each of five daily classes is scheduled use dressed up as as-needed use, which is exactly the pattern benzodiazepines are meant to avoid.
wrongExplanations.1: Atenolol shares propranolol's problem here and is additionally more cardioselective and less useful for the somatic tremor and sweating of performance anxiety.
wrongExplanations.2: Hydroxyzine is a reasonable as-needed anxiolytic with no abuse potential, but it is sedating — a genuine hazard for someone teaching all day — and it does not treat the underlying disorder, only blunts episodes.
wrongExplanations.3: This is the trap. Beta-blockers are the correct answer for the circumscribed, performance-only subtype, where exposure is occasional. His fear extends well beyond performance into restaurants and family gatherings, and he encounters it five times daily, so the episodic strategy fails on both counts.

questions.eli5: Propranolol is the famous answer for stage fright, but that works when you face the fear once in a while. He faces it five times every single day and outside work too, so he needs a daily medicine that treats the whole condition.

questions.stem: On the GAD-7 questionnaire, which of the following total score thresholds is generally taken to indicate a probable diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder warranting further clinical evaluation?
questions.explanation: A GAD-7 total of 10 or greater is the accepted cut point suggesting probable generalized anxiety disorder that warrants confirmatory clinical evaluation. Board pearl — scores of 5, 10, and 15 serve as the rough severity anchors for mild, moderate, and severe once the diagnosis is under consideration, so 10 does double duty as both the screening threshold and the moderate anchor. Do not confuse the GAD-7 with the PHQ-9, which screens for depression, or with the MMSE and MoCA, which are scored out of 30 and assess cognition.  [Learning objectives: LO 036]

wrongExplanations.0: 5 is the anchor for mild anxiety severity, not the threshold suggesting a probable diagnosis; screening at this level would flag a large proportion of the general population.
wrongExplanations.2: 12 is not one of the established anchors or cut points for this instrument.
wrongExplanations.3: 15 is the anchor for severe anxiety. Using it as the diagnostic threshold would miss the moderate range in which most patients who warrant evaluation actually score.
wrongExplanations.4: 18 is not an established threshold and sits near the instrument's ceiling of 21, so it would identify only the most extreme presentations.

questions.eli5: The GAD-7 is a short anxiety questionnaire. A score of 10 or higher is the line where a doctor should stop and look more carefully for generalized anxiety disorder.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with generalized anxiety disorder has taken sertraline for 10 weeks, titrated to 200 mg PO daily (dose range 25 to 200 mg PO daily). Her worry, irritability, and muscle tension have improved substantially but she continues to describe restlessness and difficulty falling asleep on most nights, which interferes with her work as a dispatcher. She has a history of alcohol use disorder in sustained remission for 3 years and attends weekly mutual-support meetings; she asks whether there is 'something to take the edge off,' noting that a walk-in clinic once gave her alprazolam and it 'worked instantly.' She takes no other medications. Pulse is 74/min and blood pressure is 116/72 mm Hg; physical examination and serum studies including thyroid-stimulating hormone are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?
choices: D. Increase sertraline above 200 mg PO daily
questions.explanation: Two constraints do the work. First, she is already at sertraline's maximum dose, so there is no room to escalate. Second, she has alcohol use disorder in remission, which makes any benzodiazepine a poor choice given cross-dependence and abuse potential. Buspirone is a 5-HT1A partial agonist with no sedation and no addictive potential, and it is a listed option for generalized anxiety disorder both as monotherapy and as an add-on to a baseline antidepressant for further anxiety control. Board pearl — a partial response to a maximally dosed antidepressant calls for augmentation, not abandonment of an agent that is clearly working.  [Learning objectives: LO 036, 081]

wrongExplanations.1: Alprazolam has the shortest half-life and highest abuse potential in its class, and her request framed around how fast it worked is itself a caution flag in a patient with a substance use history. Benzodiazepines are intended for short-term, as-needed use, not for ongoing residual anxiety.
wrongExplanations.2: Diazepam is long-acting with active metabolites that accumulate, and it carries the same cross-dependence problem with her alcohol use disorder. Its recognized role is alcohol withdrawal taper, not maintenance anxiolysis.
wrongExplanations.3: 200 mg daily is the top of sertraline's approved range, so this option asks for a dose that does not exist on the label and adds adverse-effect risk with no expected additional benefit.
wrongExplanations.4: Cross-tapering to another SSRI discards a substantial, documented partial response to reach for a same-mechanism agent. Paroxetine additionally has the shortest half-life and the worst discontinuation syndrome in the class.

questions.eli5: Her antidepressant is already maxed out and mostly working, so the answer is to add something rather than change it. Because she is in recovery from alcohol, the calming pills she is asking for are off the table, and buspirone eases anxiety without being habit-forming.

questions.stem: The patient described above is started on the selected agent and her as-needed alprazolam is discontinued. She returns 4 days later and states, 'This new pill does absolutely nothing — it is like taking water.' She confirms she has taken every dose as prescribed and has had no nausea, sedation, or other adverse effects. Which of the following best explains her experience?
choices: A. She has developed pharmacodynamic tolerance to the new agent within 4 days
B. Residual alprazolam is displacing the new agent from a shared binding site
C. She is experiencing benzodiazepine discontinuation syndrome that masks the new agent
D. A serum concentration should be drawn to confirm that dosing is adequate
E. The agent has no activity at the GABA-A receptor and requires 4 to 6 weeks to work
questions.explanation: Buspirone is a partial agonist at the 5-HT1A serotonin receptor and has no activity at the GABA-A receptor, which is exactly why it produces no sedation, no euphoria, and no dependence. It is also why it does nothing acutely: like an antidepressant, it needs roughly 4 to 6 weeks to produce its anxiolytic effect. Board pearl — the phrase patients use after switching off a benzodiazepine is almost verbatim 'it is like water,' because they are comparing a drug with no immediate subjective effect against one that worked within 30 minutes. Set that expectation before the switch, or the patient stops the medication before it can work.  [Learning objectives: LO 081]

wrongExplanations.0: Tolerance requires receptor or signaling adaptation over repeated exposure and could not develop to a therapeutic effect that has not yet appeared. There is nothing to become tolerant to at day 4.
wrongExplanations.1: Alprazolam acts at the benzodiazepine site on the GABA-A receptor while buspirone acts at 5-HT1A — different receptors entirely, so no competitive displacement is possible.
wrongExplanations.2: Discontinuation syndrome would produce active symptoms such as rebound anxiety, insomnia, tremor, or in severe cases seizures. She describes the absence of any effect, not the presence of new ones, and reports no adverse effects at all.
wrongExplanations.3: Buspirone is not dosed to a serum concentration; unlike lithium or valproate, it has no established therapeutic drug-monitoring range, and a level would not explain a delayed-onset mechanism.

questions.eli5: Her old anxiety pill worked in half an hour, so the new one feels like nothing. The new one works on a completely different switch in the brain and needs about a month to build up before she feels any benefit.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother because he has refused to board the school bus on 11 of the past 14 school days. He tells his mother that 'bad men' will break into the house and take her while he is gone, and he telephones her from the school nurse's office to confirm she is unhurt. On school mornings he reports stomachaches and headaches that resolve completely once he is allowed to stay home, and on weekends he has no complaints. He sleeps in his mother's doorway several nights per week. His mother notes that she herself was 'exactly the same way' as a child. He speaks freely with the physician, makes appropriate eye contact, reciprocates conversation, and plays cooperatively with his younger sister; his teachers describe him as talkative and socially engaged in class when he does attend. Developmental milestones were met on time. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Every element points at separation itself: worry that harm will befall an attachment figure, reluctance to leave home, school refusal, sleeping near the parent, and somatic complaints that appear on school mornings and vanish when he is allowed to stay home — the classic feigned illness pattern. Separation anxiety disorder affects about 4% of school-aged children, is more common in girls, and runs in families, often in close-knit ones where a parent's own separation anxiety is copied by the child; his mother's remark is that familial clue. Board pearl — treatment starts by identifying the trigger and using therapy plus family therapy, with a serotonergic antidepressant added only alongside behavioral work, never as the sole intervention.  [Learning objectives: LO 035]

wrongExplanations.0: Autism spectrum disorder requires social communication deficits plus restricted, repetitive behaviors. He makes eye contact, reciprocates conversation, plays cooperatively, and is described as socially engaged at school — the explicit negatives that close this option.
wrongExplanations.1: Generalized anxiety disorder requires excessive worry across multiple domains for more than 6 months. His worry has a single theme, and he is symptom-free on weekends when no separation is required.
wrongExplanations.2: Selective mutism is a consistent failure to speak in one specific setting despite normal speech elsewhere, lasting at least 1 month. He speaks freely with the physician and is described as talkative in class.
wrongExplanations.4: A specific phobia is fear of a discrete object or situation such as an animal, heights, or injections. School buses and school itself are the route of separation here, not the feared object; he fears what will happen to his mother in his absence.

questions.eli5: His stomachaches only show up on school mornings and disappear the moment he gets to stay home, and what he is actually scared of is that something will happen to his mom while he is away. Being afraid of being apart from a parent, not of school itself, is separation anxiety disorder.

questions.stem: A second-year medical student is hungry midway through a 2-hour lecture but remains seated. Afterward she explains that she stayed partly because gathering her belongings and finding her seat again would have been inconvenient for her, but mostly because standing up and walking out would have disrupted her classmates and been disrespectful to the lecturer. In Freud's structural model, the second consideration is best attributed to which of the following?
questions.explanation: Freud's structural model has three parts. The id is the raw, unfiltered drive — here, the impulse to get up and get food immediately. The ego supplies primitive, practical restraint that lets a person function in society, which is the first reason she gives: leaving and returning would be inconvenient for her. The superego adds the fine-tuned social and moral layer on top of that, which is the second reason: leaving would disturb others and disrespect the lecturer. Board pearl — the split to hold onto is that the ego restrains for practical reasons and the superego restrains for moral and social ones; defense mechanisms are the unconscious tools the ego uses to keep conflict among these three from overwhelming the person.  [Learning objectives: LO 061]

wrongExplanations.0: The id is the unfiltered drive itself — the hunger pushing her to leave right now. It is what the other two structures are restraining, not the source of restraint.
wrongExplanations.1: The ego accounts for her first reason, the practical inconvenience of leaving and returning. It provides basic reality-testing restraint but not the moral weighing of how her exit would affect other people.
wrongExplanations.3: The unconscious is a level of awareness in Freud's topographic model, not a structure in the structural model, and it does not describe a moral restraint on behavior.
wrongExplanations.4: The preconscious likewise belongs to the topographic model and refers to material accessible to awareness but not currently in it — it is not an agency that restrains action.

questions.eli5: One part of her wanted food right away. Another part said leaving would be a hassle for her. The part that said it would be rude to the teacher and the class is the superego, the moral rule-follower.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman comes to the office 3 weeks after she was pulled from a burning apartment building in which two of her neighbors died. Since the fire she has had nightly dreams of smoke filling a hallway, intrusive images of the stairwell that arrive without warning during the day, and a startle response so pronounced that a slammed door made her drop a full tray at work. She has refused to re-enter any building with an interior stairwell and now takes a 40-minute detour to avoid the block where the fire occurred. She describes feeling 'behind glass,' as though events are happening at a distance, and she has been unable to recall how she got out of the building. She reports no hallucinations and no fixed false beliefs. She has no psychiatric history, does not drink alcohol, and urine toxicology screening is negative. Vital signs are within normal limits and physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: She has genuine Criterion A trauma exposure — actual death and threatened death — plus intrusion (nightmares, intrusive images), avoidance (stairwells, the block), arousal (exaggerated startle), and dissociation (derealization described as being behind glass, plus inability to recall her escape). The buried clue is the clock: at 3 weeks she sits inside the 3-day to 1-month window that defines acute stress disorder. Board pearl — acute stress disorder is the anxiety-chapter equivalent of brief psychotic disorder, sharing PTSD's symptom domains on a compressed timeline; if these same symptoms persist past 1 month, the diagnosis converts to PTSD without any change in what the patient is experiencing.  [Learning objectives: LO 060, 098]

wrongExplanations.1: Adjustment disorder can follow any identifiable stressor, but it is diagnosed only when the presentation does not meet criteria for another specific disorder. She has full trauma-related symptomatology after Criterion A exposure, so the more specific trauma diagnosis takes precedence.
wrongExplanations.2: Brief psychotic disorder requires at least one core psychotic symptom — delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, or grossly disorganized behavior. She explicitly reports no hallucinations and no fixed false beliefs. Derealization is a dissociative symptom with intact reality testing, not psychosis.
wrongExplanations.3: Generalized anxiety disorder requires excessive worry about multiple everyday domains for more than 6 months. Her symptoms are tethered entirely to one event 3 weeks ago.
wrongExplanations.4: Major depressive disorder requires depressed mood or anhedonia plus additional neurovegetative symptoms for at least 2 weeks. Neither core symptom is described; her presentation is intrusion, avoidance, arousal, and dissociation.
wrongExplanations.5: PTSD requires that symptoms persist for more than 1 month. At 3 weeks she has not reached that threshold, which is the single criterion separating these two diagnoses.

questions.eli5: Three weeks after escaping a deadly fire she has nightmares, jumps at loud noises, avoids stairwells, and feels like she is watching life through glass. Under one month, this exact picture is called acute stress disorder.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman comes to the office 7 months after she was pulled from a burning apartment building in which two of her neighbors died. Since the fire she has had nightly dreams of smoke filling a hallway, intrusive images of the stairwell that arrive without warning during the day, and a startle response so pronounced that a slammed door made her drop a full tray at work. She has refused to re-enter any building with an interior stairwell and now takes a 40-minute detour to avoid the block where the fire occurred. She has become convinced that she is 'the kind of person who lets people die,' has withdrawn from her closest friends, and no longer takes the photography classes she once organized her week around. She reports no hallucinations and no fixed false beliefs. She has no psychiatric history, does not drink alcohol, and urine toxicology screening is negative. Vital signs are within normal limits and physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This is the identical presentation with one variable moved — 3 weeks becomes 7 months — and that single change converts the diagnosis. PTSD requires Criterion A trauma exposure plus intrusion (B), avoidance (C), negative alterations in cognition and mood (D), and arousal (E), all persisting beyond 1 month (F) with impairment (G) and no substance or medical explanation (H). The persistent negative self-belief that she is the kind of person who lets people die, plus social withdrawal and loss of a valued activity, supplies Criterion D, which was not required at 3 weeks. Board pearl — most acute stress disorder resolves within the first 30 days; the patients still symptomatic past that mark are the ones whose diagnosis converts.  [Learning objectives: LO 060, 098]

wrongExplanations.0: Acute stress disorder is capped at 1 month post-trauma. At 7 months she is well outside that window, and the diagnosis converts rather than persisting under the same name.
wrongExplanations.1: Adjustment disorder applies when the presentation does not meet criteria for another specific disorder, and its own timing rule expects resolution within 6 months after the stressor ends. She meets full PTSD criteria at 7 months.
wrongExplanations.2: Brief psychotic disorder requires a core psychotic symptom lasting 1 day to less than 1 month. She has neither hallucinations nor delusions, and her belief about herself is a negative self-appraisal, not a fixed false belief held against evidence.
wrongExplanations.3: Generalized anxiety disorder requires excessive worry about multiple everyday domains rather than symptoms anchored to a single traumatic event.
wrongExplanations.5: Withdrawal and loss of interest could suggest depression, but they occur here within a trauma syndrome that also includes nightmares, intrusive images, trauma-specific avoidance, and exaggerated startle — none of which major depressive disorder accounts for. Her negative cognitions are Criterion D of PTSD.

questions.eli5: Same fire, same nightmares and jumpiness, but now it has been seven months instead of three weeks, and she has started believing she is a person who lets people die. Once these symptoms last longer than a month, the name changes to PTSD.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman is brought to the office by her sister 10 weeks after her husband of 5 years left her for a younger colleague. Since then she has been tearful most days, has quit her accounting job without notice, and has begun drinking four to five glasses of wine nightly, having previously drunk only socially. She has telephoned her former husband's new partner repeatedly at night, twice leaving messages that the sister describes as 'threatening,' and last week she keyed the partner's car. She denies suicidal ideation and denies any period of elevated mood or decreased need for sleep. She has no prior psychiatric or legal history, and reports no anhedonia, appetite change, or feelings of worthlessness. Vital signs are within normal limits. Aminotransferases and complete blood count are normal, and urine toxicology screening is negative. On mental status examination, affect is tearful and reactive, and thought process is linear. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: A. Adjustment disorder with depressed mood
C. Adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood
D. Adjustment disorder with disturbance of conduct
E. Major depressive disorder, single episode
F. Adjustment disorder with mixed disturbance of emotions and conduct
questions.explanation: Adjustment disorder requires symptoms beginning within 3 months of an identifiable stressor, distress out of proportion to that stressor or clear functional impairment, and a presentation that does not meet criteria for another disorder. Her stressor was 10 weeks ago and did not have to be life-threatening — that is precisely what separates adjustment disorder from PTSD and acute stress disorder. The subtype is decided by counting what is present: she has emotional symptoms (tearfulness, low mood) AND conduct symptoms (quitting without notice, threatening calls, property destruction), which together define the mixed disturbance of emotions and conduct subtype. Board pearl — adjustment disorders are the most commonly encountered psychiatric disorders overall, and symptoms must resolve within 6 months after the stressor and its consequences end.  [Learning objectives: LO 060, 098]

wrongExplanations.0: The depressed mood subtype is used when emotional symptoms stand alone. It ignores the threatening calls and the keyed car, which are conduct symptoms that must be captured in the subtype.
wrongExplanations.1: The anxiety subtype requires nervousness, worry, or jitteriness as the predominant feature. Her presentation is tearful and behaviorally disinhibited rather than anxious.
wrongExplanations.2: This subtype combines two emotional presentations, anxiety and depressed mood. It still leaves her disturbance of conduct unaccounted for.
wrongExplanations.3: The disturbance of conduct subtype is used when behavior violating norms or the rights of others is the whole picture. She is also tearful most days, so an emotional component is present alongside the conduct.
wrongExplanations.4: Major depressive disorder requires 5 or more SIG E CAPS symptoms including depressed mood or anhedonia. She explicitly denies anhedonia, appetite change, and worthlessness, and her affect is reactive — these stated negatives keep her below the MDE threshold, which is what allows an adjustment disorder to be diagnosed at all.

questions.eli5: Ten weeks after her husband left, she is crying a lot and also doing things she never used to do, like quitting her job on the spot and scratching someone's car. Because she has both the feelings part and the behavior part, the diagnosis names both.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man who served two combat deployments is seen for follow-up of posttraumatic stress disorder. He has taken sertraline 150 mg PO daily for 5 months, with meaningful improvement in intrusive daytime memories and avoidance. He continues to have vivid combat nightmares four to five nights weekly that wake him in a panic, after which he patrols the house before he can lie back down; his wife has moved to the guest room. He denies hallucinations, denies suicidal ideation, and has no history of substance use. Pulse is 68/min and blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg supine; physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to his regimen?
questions.explanation: The PTSD pharmacotherapy algorithm branches first on the sleep complaint. Sleep disturbed by nightmares and nighttime hyperarousal gets prazosin, an alpha-1 adrenergic blocker; sleep-onset difficulty without nightmares gets trazodone. Only after that does the algorithm proceed to an SSRI trial, then a second SSRI, SNRI, or mirtazapine, with an antipsychotic added only if psychosis is present. His SSRI is already working on the daytime cluster, so the correct move targets the residual symptom specifically. Board pearl — prazosin for PTSD nightmares is a board favorite precisely because the drug is better known for benign prostatic hyperplasia and hypertension; check for orthostasis when starting it.  [Learning objectives: LO 076]

wrongExplanations.0: Clonidine is an alpha-2 agonist listed as an augmenting option for the hyperarousal cluster generally, but prazosin is the agent specifically indicated for nightmares and nighttime hyperarousal and is the first branch point in the algorithm.
wrongExplanations.1: Benzodiazepines are generally avoided in PTSD — they do not meaningfully improve core symptoms, carry dependence risk, and diazepam's long half-life and active metabolites make it a particularly poor choice for chronic nightly use.
wrongExplanations.2: Mirtazapine appears in the algorithm only after a second SSRI or SNRI trial, and it is a global antidepressant-plus-sedative strategy rather than a targeted treatment for nightmares. His SSRI is already producing meaningful benefit.
wrongExplanations.4: Quetiapine is an augmentation option for the hyperarousal cluster, but antipsychotics are reserved for later steps or for the presence of psychosis, which he explicitly denies. It also carries metabolic and sedation burden that prazosin does not.

questions.eli5: His main medicine is already helping during the day, but the combat nightmares are still waking him up every night. Prazosin, a blood-pressure pill, is the specific medicine known to quiet trauma nightmares.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman has been given a diagnosis of panic disorder after a negative cardiac and pulmonary evaluation. She is started on the medication class considered first-line for long-term control of this disorder and is scheduled for follow-up in 4 weeks. She asks what to expect. Which of the following is the most appropriate statement to make to this patient?
choices: A. "This works within 30 minutes, so take one only when you feel an attack beginning."
B. "You may have stomach upset and feel more anxious in the first week or two, before the benefit arrives at four to six weeks."
C. "You will need to avoid aged cheeses, cured meats, and draft beer for as long as you take this."
D. "We will draw a blood level in five days and adjust your dose based on the result."
E. "Stopping this abruptly can cause a withdrawal seizure, so it is critical never to miss a dose."
questions.explanation: Two inferential steps, with the middle one unstated: panic disorder's first-line long-term pharmacotherapy is an SSRI (short-acting benzodiazepines are reserved for the acute attack), and the counseling point that matters most for an SSRI is the mismatch in timing. The transporter is blocked the moment the first dose is taken, so serotonin floods the synapse immediately and hits gastrointestinal and other peripheral targets right away — but postsynaptic receptors need roughly 4 to 6 weeks to adapt before the patient feels better. Board pearl — this is why side effects appear in weeks 1 to 2 while benefit appears at weeks 4 to 6, and why 'I have taken it two weeks and feel no different' is an expected course rather than treatment failure. Warning the patient in advance is what keeps them from stopping during the worst window.  [Learning objectives: LO 050, 073, 076]

wrongExplanations.0: This describes a short-acting benzodiazepine used as needed for an attack in progress. Benzodiazepines are not the first-line long-term treatment for panic disorder, and instructing a patient to take a daily SSRI only during attacks would make it ineffective.
wrongExplanations.2: Tyramine restriction applies to MAOIs, where dietary tyramine can precipitate a hypertensive crisis. MAOIs are fourth-line antidepressants and are not first-line for panic disorder.
wrongExplanations.3: Serum concentration monitoring applies to lithium, valproate, and carbamazepine. SSRIs have no established therapeutic drug-monitoring range and are titrated to clinical response and tolerability.
wrongExplanations.4: Abrupt discontinuation of an SSRI causes a discontinuation syndrome — flu-like symptoms, dizziness, brain zaps, irritability — not a withdrawal seizure. Withdrawal seizures are the danger with abrupt cessation of benzodiazepines, barbiturates, or alcohol.

questions.eli5: The pill starts changing her brain chemistry the very first day, which is why upset stomach and jitters show up right away. Feeling better takes about a month, so she needs to know the rough part comes first.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man has a 2-year history of intrusive thoughts that his hands are contaminated with fecal bacteria. He washes them until they crack and bleed, currently spending about 3 hours daily on washing rituals, and he is emphatic that the thoughts are 'stupid and irrational — I know they are not true, and I hate that I do this.' Twelve weeks ago he was started on fluoxetine 20 mg PO daily and has taken every dose. His washing has decreased from 5 hours to about 3 hours daily and he reports the obsessions are 'a little quieter,' but he is still late to class most days. He has had no nausea, insomnia, sexual dysfunction, or other adverse effects. He has no cardiac history, no seizure history, and does not use alcohol or illicit drugs. Vital signs are within normal limits. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?
choices: E. Increase fluoxetine toward the maximum dose
questions.explanation: The trap is reading a partial response at 12 weeks as a failed trial. It is not a failed trial, because he was never at an OCD dose. Obsessive-compulsive disorder requires substantially higher SSRI doses than depression does, and 20 mg of fluoxetine is a standard depression starting dose. He is improving and has no adverse effects at all, which means the dose has room to move. Board pearl — the discriminator confirming OCD here is that the obsessions are ego-dystonic: he recognizes them as irrational and unwanted, which separates OCD from obsessive-compulsive personality disorder, where the traits are ego-syntonic and the patient sees nothing wrong with them.  [Learning objectives: LO 036, 081]

wrongExplanations.0: Benzodiazepines have limited benefit in OCD and do not treat obsessions or compulsions. Adding one exposes a 22-year-old to dependence risk while leaving an underdosed SSRI in place.
wrongExplanations.1: Adjunctive antipsychotics are reserved for OCD that remains resistant after multiple adequate trials of SSRIs or clomipramine. He has not yet completed even one adequate trial, since the dose has never reached the OCD range.
wrongExplanations.2: Clomipramine is the established alternative for OCD, but cross-tapering abandons an agent that is producing measurable improvement without adverse effects, and it trades a clean SSRI for a tricyclic with anticholinergic and cardiac liabilities.
wrongExplanations.3: Bupropion is not an effective treatment for OCD — it has no serotonergic activity at all — and its activating profile can worsen anxiety.

questions.eli5: He is getting better on his medicine and having no side effects, but he is on a depression-sized dose. Obsessive-compulsive disorder needs a much bigger dose of the same drug, so you climb the dose before you change anything.

questions.stem: Marcus is a 38-year-old estate attorney whose partners have asked him to seek an evaluation. He redrafts routine documents six or seven times to perfect the formatting and has missed three filing deadlines as a result. He keeps every draft of every file going back 12 years and will not let the office discard any of them. He has not taken a vacation in 9 years, describes weekends as 'wasted time,' and refuses to delegate because no associate will 'do it the correct way.' He lives well below his means and reuses envelopes. He denies any unwanted intrusive thoughts and denies performing any repetitive act to relieve anxiety. When his partners' concerns are described to him, he appears puzzled and states that his standards are 'simply the correct way to practice law' and that the firm's real problem is everyone else's carelessness. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This is a pervasive, lifelong pattern of perfectionism that interferes with task completion, excessive devotion to work at the expense of leisure, inability to delegate, miserliness, and inability to discard worn-out or worthless objects — the LOW MIRTH picture of obsessive-compulsive personality disorder. The decisive discriminator is in the last two sentences: he has no true obsessions or compulsions, and the traits are ego-syntonic. He sees no problem with himself and locates the problem in everyone else. Board pearl — OCD is ego-dystonic and the patient wants the thoughts gone; OCPD is ego-syntonic and the patient wants the world to meet his standard. That single distinction decides this pair every time.  [Learning objectives: LO 036, 041]

wrongExplanations.0: Generalized anxiety disorder requires excessive, difficult-to-control worry across multiple everyday domains for more than 6 months with associated symptoms such as restlessness, fatigue, and muscle tension. His presentation is a rigid character style, not a worry syndrome.
wrongExplanations.1: Hoarding disorder involves persistent difficulty discarding possessions with accumulation that congests living areas and causes distress at the thought of parting with them. His retention of files is one facet of a broader rigid, controlling pattern that also includes perfectionism, workaholism, and miserliness.
wrongExplanations.3: Obsessive-compulsive disorder requires true obsessions — intrusive, unwanted, ego-dystonic thoughts — and compulsions performed to neutralize anxiety, typically consuming more than an hour daily. He explicitly denies both, and he does not experience his behavior as unwanted.
wrongExplanations.4: Avoidant personality disorder centers on fear of criticism and rejection with a longing for connection despite avoidance. He is not avoiding others out of fear; he is confidently critical of them.

questions.eli5: He redoes everything until it is perfect, never takes a break, saves every scrap of paper, and thinks his way is simply correct. Because he does not think anything is wrong with him, this is the personality version, not the anxiety disorder version.

questions.stem: Which of the following disorders is classified in the DSM-5 chapter on obsessive-compulsive and related disorders rather than in the anxiety disorders chapter?
questions.explanation: DSM-5 split what had been a single anxiety disorders chapter into three. The anxiety disorders chapter retains separation anxiety disorder, selective mutism, specific phobia, social anxiety disorder, panic disorder, and generalized anxiety disorder. The obsessive-compulsive and related disorders chapter contains OCD, body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding disorder, trichotillomania, and excoriation (skin-picking) disorder. The third chapter, trauma- and stressor-related disorders, holds reactive attachment disorder, disinhibited social engagement disorder, PTSD, acute stress disorder, and the adjustment disorders. Board pearl — the newer OCD-spectrum entries are all treated with serotonergic agents plus CBT, which is a useful way to remember they cluster together.  [Learning objectives: LO 036]

wrongExplanations.1: Generalized anxiety disorder remains in the anxiety disorders chapter; it is defined by excessive worry for more than 6 months with 3 or more of 6 associated symptoms.
wrongExplanations.2: Panic disorder remains in the anxiety disorders chapter, and DSM-5 additionally unlinked it from agoraphobia so the two are now separate co-occurring diagnoses.
wrongExplanations.3: Selective mutism was moved into the anxiety disorders chapter in DSM-5 and is defined by consistent failure to speak in one specific setting despite normal speech elsewhere for at least 1 month.
wrongExplanations.4: Separation anxiety disorder is also in the anxiety disorders chapter; DSM-5 removed the requirement that onset be in childhood, so it can now be diagnosed in adults.

questions.eli5: DSM-5 split one big anxiety chapter into three. Skin-picking sits with obsessive-compulsive disorder and hair-pulling in the OCD group; the other four choices stayed in the anxiety group.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with Child-Pugh class B cirrhosis from prior alcohol use, abstinent for 5 years, is admitted for elective inguinal hernia repair. He develops marked situational anxiety the evening before surgery, with restlessness and an inability to sleep, and the surgical team requests a short-term anxiolytic. He has no history of an anxiety disorder. Serum albumin is 3.0 g/dL, total bilirubin is 2.1 mg/dL, and INR is 1.4. Pulse is 78/min and blood pressure is 122/76 mm Hg. There is no asterixis and he is fully oriented. Which of the following is the most appropriate agent?
questions.explanation: Most benzodiazepines are metabolized by hepatic phase I oxidation into active metabolites, so impaired hepatic function lets both parent drug and metabolites accumulate. Three agents skip phase I entirely and undergo direct phase II glucuronidation — lorazepam, oxazepam, and temazepam, the LOT benzodiazepines — making them the preferred choice in liver impairment and in older adults. Lorazepam is the only LOT agent on this list, and it additionally has an intermediate half-life appropriate for short-term perioperative anxiety. Board pearl — the same reasoning makes LOT agents the choice for alcohol withdrawal in a patient with significant liver disease, and older adults need lower doses generally because increased body fat expands the volume of distribution for these lipophilic drugs.  [Learning objectives: LO 073, 091]

wrongExplanations.0: Alprazolam undergoes hepatic oxidation, has the shortest half-life and highest abuse potential in the class, and its use in a patient with a history of alcohol use disorder is additionally undesirable.
wrongExplanations.1: Chlordiazepoxide is long-acting with active metabolites generated by hepatic oxidation. Its recognized role is the uncomplicated alcohol detoxification taper in a patient with intact liver function, not perioperative anxiolysis in cirrhosis.
wrongExplanations.2: Clonazepam is fairly long-acting and depends on hepatic oxidative metabolism, so it would accumulate in this patient.
wrongExplanations.4: Diazepam is the worst choice here: long half-life, active metabolites, hepatic oxidation, and marked accumulation in older adults — the lecture note is explicitly to reduce the dose in the elderly.
wrongExplanations.5: Midazolam is ultra-short-acting and used for procedural sedation and anesthetic induction, not for overnight anxiety on the ward, and it also depends on hepatic oxidative metabolism.

questions.eli5: Most calming medicines have to be broken down by the liver in two steps, and his liver is scarred. Lorazepam skips the step his liver is bad at, so it does not pile up in his body.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man is hospitalized after a motor vehicle collision in which another driver ran a red light and struck his car, causing multiple facial lacerations. Throughout the admission he speaks about the other driver without apparent resentment, remarking that 'accidents happen and he was probably having a bad day.' After the plastic surgery service repairs his lacerations, he becomes intensely angry about a 2-cm residual scar along his jaw, files two formal complaints against the surgeon, and demands that she be removed from his care. He has no psychiatric history, and his affect is otherwise appropriate and reactive. Which of the following defense mechanisms best explains his behavior?
questions.explanation: Displacement redirects an emotion from its true, often threatening or unreachable target onto a safer, more available one. His anger belongs to the driver who caused the collision, but that driver is absent and confronting him would mean confronting the helplessness of the event itself. The surgeon is present, accessible, and safe to be angry at, so the affect lands on her and attaches to a trivial scar. Board pearl — the tell for displacement is affect that is disproportionate to its stated target while an obvious, unaddressed target sits elsewhere in the story; the classic textbook version is snapping at a spouse after a bad day with a difficult boss.  [Learning objectives: LO 058]

wrongExplanations.0: Denial is refusal to accept an unbearable piece of external reality, such as insisting nothing is wrong and skipping a recommended workup. He fully acknowledges the collision and its consequences.
wrongExplanations.2: Identification is unconsciously patterning one's own behavior after someone more powerful, as when a person bullied by a coach becomes a harsh coach. He is not modeling himself on anyone.
wrongExplanations.3: Projection attributes one's own unacceptable feelings or impulses to someone else — a person who cheated becoming convinced everyone else cheats. He is not attributing his anger to the surgeon; he is directing his anger at her.
wrongExplanations.4: Repression is the involuntary, unconscious blocking of a distressing memory from awareness entirely. He recalls the collision clearly and discusses it without difficulty.
wrongExplanations.5: Sublimation is a mature defense channeling an unacceptable impulse into a socially productive outlet, such as aggressive impulses expressed through competitive contact sport. Filing complaints against a treating physician is not a productive channeling of the impulse.

questions.eli5: He is not angry at the driver who actually hit him — he is angry at the surgeon over a small scar. The feeling belonged somewhere else and got aimed at a safer target.

questions.stem: Which of the following best distinguishes suppression from repression?
choices: A. Suppression converts the feeling into a physical symptom, whereas repression does not
B. Suppression occurs only in personality disorders, whereas repression occurs in healthy adults
C. Suppression redirects the feeling onto a safer target, whereas repression removes it entirely
D. Suppression is characteristic of childhood, whereas repression emerges in adulthood
E. Suppression is deliberate and conscious, whereas repression is involuntary and unconscious
questions.explanation: Suppression is the conscious, deliberate postponement of attention to a disturbing thought or feeling — a surgeon consciously setting aside a personal worry to focus during an operation. It is the only defense with a conscious component, which is part of why it is classified as one of the four mature defenses (Sublimation, Altruism, Suppression, Humor — 'mature adults wear a SASH'). Repression is its involuntary, unconscious counterpart: a distressing memory is blocked from awareness entirely, as when an adult has no recollection of a difficult period in childhood. Board pearl — this pair is the single most commonly confused item in the defense mechanism list, and the mature four are far likelier to be the correct answer than a distractor.  [Learning objectives: LO 058]

wrongExplanations.0: Converting emotional conflict into a physical symptom describes conversion, a separate and less mature defense, not suppression.
wrongExplanations.1: Both defenses occur across the full range of psychological health. Suppression in particular is classified as mature and is characteristic of well-functioning adults, so the claim is reversed.
wrongExplanations.2: Redirecting a feeling onto a safer target describes displacement. Neither suppression nor repression involves changing the target of the emotion; both act on awareness of it.
wrongExplanations.3: Neither defense is defined by developmental stage. Fixation and regression are the pair defined by developmental position — fixation is being stuck at an earlier stage, regression is sliding back to one already passed.

questions.eli5: Suppression is when you decide on purpose to put a worry aside until later. Repression is when your mind hides something from you without asking, and you do not even know it is gone.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is seen by the psychiatry consultation-liaison service on hospital day 4 following an anterior myocardial infarction treated with percutaneous coronary intervention. He is tearful during the interview and states, 'I have been a roofer for thirty-two years. I do not know who I am if I cannot work.' He reports poor sleep on the unit and worry about his mortgage. He has no psychiatric history, no prior trauma, and no history of self-harm. He denies suicidal ideation, denies anhedonia, and scores 8 on the PHQ-9, and his symptoms do not meet criteria for a major depressive episode. He is medically stable and is expected to be discharged in 2 days to cardiac rehabilitation. Which of the following psychotherapeutic approaches is most appropriate at this point?
choices: C. Eye movement desensitization and reprocessing
questions.explanation: Supportive psychotherapy — listening, encouragement, and stability — is the approach matched to acute crises, acute medical comorbidity, and acute stressors, and it is essentially what consultation-liaison psychiatry delivers at the bedside. The constraint here is the setting and the clock: a medically ill man 4 days out from an infarction, facing an identity threat, discharging in 48 hours. CBT is the correct default for most outpatient presentations, but a course of structured skills work is not what fits a 2-day inpatient window. Board pearl — the 10-second modality picker is BPD gets DBT, trauma gets EMDR, relationship problems get IPT, acute crisis or medical illness gets supportive, and everything else gets CBT.  [Learning objectives: LO 002, 009, 011, 012]

wrongExplanations.0: CBT is the broad default and would be entirely reasonable as outpatient follow-up, but it is a structured skills-based course requiring multiple sessions. It is not the approach for a man in acute distress who leaves the hospital in 2 days, and he does not meet criteria for the depressive disorder CBT would be targeting.
wrongExplanations.1: DBT was created by Marsha Linehan specifically for borderline personality disorder and is chosen when that diagnosis is present. He has no psychiatric history and no pattern of unstable identity, relationships, or self-harm.
wrongExplanations.2: EMDR is trauma-focused, used when reminders of a traumatic event trigger a misattributed fight-or-flight response. The stem states he has no prior trauma, and an uncomplicated revascularized infarction with an identity concern is not a trauma-reprocessing problem.
wrongExplanations.4: IPT is a structured, manualized, time-limited therapy for patients whose central problem is current interpersonal relationships and communication. His distress concerns occupational identity and finances, not a relational conflict.
wrongExplanations.5: Psychodynamic psychotherapy is exploratory and long-course, using free association and transference. It is poorly suited to an acute inpatient crisis with a 2-day horizon.

questions.eli5: Four days after a heart attack, he is scared and grieving the work that made him who he is, and he goes home in two days. What helps right now is someone steady who listens and reassures, not a long course of homework and skills.
